NB001.why: A key, password or connection string in code is copied into Git, notebook versions, cell outputs and anything else that keeps the notebook. Anyone who can read the notebook can use it.
NB001.fine: Never in a notebook that is saved or shared. Rotate a secret that was committed.
NB001.principle: Keep secrets out of code, and read them from a vault when the code runs.
NB001.impact: Security. Anyone who can read the notebook, its versions or its Git history can use the secret.
NB001.check: Best practices shows no NB001, and the Git page's secret check finds nothing before you commit. A secret that was ever committed stays in history, so rotate it.

NB002.why: An `abfss://<workspace id>@...` path points at one workspace. When the notebook is promoted to Test or Prod, it still reads and writes the Dev lakehouse.
NB002.fine: A one-off notebook that is never promoted. A parameter is still easier to change.
NB002.principle: Let the environment decide where data lives. Code names tables, not workspaces.
NB002.impact: Reliability. After promotion, Test or Prod reads and writes the Dev lakehouse.
NB002.check: No path in the notebook holds a workspace or lakehouse id. After you promote it and run it once, the write shows in the Test lakehouse's table history, not Dev's.
NB002.after: df = spark.read.table("sales")          # or the default lakehouse's "Tables/sales"

NB003.why: Both bring every row to the driver, one machine. A table that fits today can run the driver out of memory next month.
NB003.fine: The DataFrame is already small by construction, such as the result of an aggregation.
NB003.principle: Move the work to the data, not all the data to one machine.
NB003.impact: Reliability. The driver can run out of memory as the table grows, and the run fails.
NB003.check: The finding is gone, and the rows brought back are capped by the limit or by the number of groups.
NB003.after:
rows = df.groupBy("region").agg(F.sum("amount")).toPandas()   # aggregate first
sample = df.limit(1000).toPandas()                              # or take a sample

NB004.why: Nobody reads a scheduled run's output, and displaying a whole table makes the run slower and its output large. Checked only for notebooks that run on a schedule.
NB004.principle: A scheduled run's output is a log. Keep it short.
NB004.impact: Performance. The run is slower and its saved output is large.
NB004.check: The scheduled run's output shows a count or a sample, not the whole table.

NB005.why: Inferring a schema reads the files an extra time, and the inferred types change when the files do, so a column can turn from a number into a string without warning.
NB005.principle: Say what shape you expect the data to have, instead of guessing it from the files.
NB005.impact: Reliability and performance. The files are read an extra time, and a column's type can change without warning.
NB005.check: `df.printSchema()` shows the types you wrote, on every run.
NB005.after:
schema = "order_id INT, order_date DATE, amount DECIMAL(18,2)"
df = spark.read.option("header", True).schema(schema).csv("Files/orders/")

NB006.why: It reads every column, which costs time on wide tables, and code that depends on column order breaks when a column is added or renamed.
NB006.fine: A quick look at a table while you explore.
NB006.principle: Ask only for the columns you use.
NB006.impact: Performance on wide tables, and code that breaks when a column is added or renamed.
NB006.check: The query names its columns, and the result has the columns your code uses, in the order you named them.
NB006.after: SELECT order_id, order_date, amount FROM sales

NB007.why: An overwrite without `replaceWhere` rewrites every file and makes a full new table version, even when only one day changed.
NB007.fine: Small tables, and full reloads that are meant to replace everything.
NB007.principle: Rewrite only the data that changed.
NB007.impact: Performance and capacity. Every file is rewritten on each run, even when one day changed.
NB007.check: `DESCRIBE HISTORY` shows the write removed and added only the files of the range you replaced, and a row count outside that range is the same before and after.

NB008.why: The package is installed again on every run. That is slow, and a run fails when the package index can't be reached. Checked only for notebooks that run on a schedule.
NB008.instead: Put the package in a Fabric environment and attach it to the notebook.
NB008.principle: A scheduled run uses the same prepared environment every time.
NB008.impact: Reliability. Each run installs the package again, and fails when the package index can't be reached.
NB008.check: The notebook has no `%pip` lines, and its attached environment lists the package and its version.

NB009.why: A new release of the package can change results or break the notebook, and two runs a week apart may not use the same code.
NB009.principle: Pin what you depend on, so a run today and a run next month use the same code.
NB009.impact: Reliability. A new release can change results or break the notebook between two runs.
NB009.check: Every install line names a version (`==1.2.3`), and `%pip show` reports that version.

NB010.why: Each write makes small files and a new table version. A thousand passes make a thousand versions and a slow table.
NB010.principle: Write once per run, not once per item.
NB010.impact: Performance. Each write makes small files and a new table version.
NB010.check: `DESCRIBE HISTORY` shows one write for the run, and the table gained the same number of rows as before the change.
NB010.after:
from functools import reduce
from pyspark.sql import DataFrame
reduce(DataFrame.unionByName, [load(r) for r in regions]).write.mode("append").saveAsTable("sales")

NB011.why: Every `count()` runs the whole query again. Three counts read the data three times.
NB011.principle: Work a value out once and keep it.
NB011.impact: Performance. Each `count()` reads the data again.
NB011.check: The cell starts one count job for the DataFrame instead of several (the Spark jobs listed under the cell).

NB012.why: `except ...: pass` hides a failure, so the run reports success while the table is wrong or missing.
NB012.principle: Fail loudly, or handle only the errors you expect and say that you did.
NB012.impact: Reliability. The run reports success while a table is wrong or missing.
NB012.check: Make the expected error happen once (a missing file, for example) and see the message. Any other error still fails the run.

NB018.why: A Python UDF sends every row from Spark to a Python process and back, one row at a time. A built-in function runs inside Spark and is usually many times faster. When nothing built in fits, a `pandas_udf` works on whole batches. `pandas_udf` and Fabric User Data Functions (`@udf.function()`) aren't flagged.
NB018.fine: Logic no built-in function can express, on a small table.
NB018.principle: Use the engine's own functions before writing your own.
NB018.impact: Performance. Every row goes to Python and back.
NB018.check: Run the cell before and after on the same data (Prove, or Side by side) and check the rows match. Compare the measured times of the two runs.
NB018.before:
upper = F.udf(lambda s: s.upper())
df = df.withColumn("name", upper("name"))

NB019.why: Spark's readers expect storage paths, so an `http(s)` address fails or reads differently from run to run, and the file behind it can change or disappear. A copy in the lakehouse gives every run the same input. Reading a web address with pandas (`pd.read_csv(url)`) isn't flagged.
NB019.principle: Land outside data first, then read your own copy.
NB019.impact: Reliability. A read from the web can fail, or read a different file, from one run to the next.
NB019.check: The read path is under `Files/`, and two runs read the same file.
NB019.after:
# copy it once (a pipeline Copy activity, for example), then read the copy
df = spark.read.option("header", True).csv("Files/landing/sales.csv")

NB020.why: `VACUUM` deletes files that older table versions use. With less than the default 168 hours, it can delete files a running query or write still needs, and time travel to those versions stops working. Found in `%%sql` cells, `spark.sql(...)`, `DeltaTable.vacuum(hours)` and delta-rs `vacuum(retention_hours=...)`.
NB020.fine: A table nothing else reads or writes, such as a scratch table in a test.
NB020.principle: Keep enough history for anything that may still read it.
NB020.impact: Data loss. A running read or write can fail, and time travel to older versions stops working.
NB020.check: `VACUUM` keeps 168 hours or more, and `DESCRIBE HISTORY` still lists the versions you need.

SQ001.why: The object's columns change whenever the table's do. A report or caller that expects the old columns breaks, and a view can keep returning the columns it had when it was created.
SQ001.principle: A view's columns are a promise to its callers. Name them.
SQ001.impact: Reliability. Reports and callers break when the table's columns change.
SQ001.check: The view's columns in the explorer are the ones you named, and they stay the same after a column is added to the table.
SQ001.before: CREATE VIEW dbo.v_sales AS SELECT * FROM dbo.sales;
SQ001.after: CREATE VIEW dbo.v_sales AS SELECT order_id, order_date, amount FROM dbo.sales;

SQ002.why: The engine skips files and row groups by comparing a column's values with your filter. Wrapped in a function, the column can't be compared directly, so every row is read.
SQ002.fine: Small tables, or a function on the other side of the comparison (`order_date >= DATEADD(day, -7, GETDATE())`), which isn't reported.
SQ002.principle: Compare the column itself with a value or a range. Put any function on the value's side, so the engine can skip the data it doesn't need.
SQ002.impact: Performance. Every row is read, whatever the filter keeps.
SQ002.check: Where Try the fix is offered, Compare runs both versions read-only and shows whether the rows match, with each run's measured time.

SQ003.why: In a Fabric Warehouse, MAX columns are stored and read less efficiently than sized ones, and tools that read the table can't plan for the length.
SQ003.fine: Values that really can be longer than 8,000 bytes, like JSON documents.
SQ003.principle: Size each column for the values it holds.
SQ003.impact: Performance. MAX columns are stored and read less efficiently, and tools can't plan for their length.
SQ003.check: `SELECT MAX(LEN(name)) FROM dbo.customer` fits inside the size you chose.

SQ004.why: The new table takes its types from the query, so a change to the query or the data can change the table's types. `#temp` tables aren't reported.
SQ004.principle: Declare a table's column types. Don't let a query guess them.
SQ004.impact: Maintenance. A change to the query or the data can change the table's types.
SQ004.check: The table's columns in the explorer have the types you declared.
SQ004.before: SELECT order_id, amount INTO dbo.big_orders FROM dbo.sales WHERE amount > 1000;
SQ004.after:
CREATE TABLE dbo.big_orders (order_id int, amount decimal(18,2));
INSERT INTO dbo.big_orders (order_id, amount) SELECT order_id, amount FROM dbo.sales WHERE amount > 1000;

SQ005.why: `sales` means whatever the caller's default schema has, which differs between people and service accounts. `dbo.sales` always means the same table.
SQ005.principle: Name the schema with every table, so the query means the same thing whoever runs it.
SQ005.impact: Reliability. Two people, or a person and a service account, can read different tables.
SQ005.check: Every table name has a schema. Where Try the fix is offered, Compare shows both versions return the same rows.

SQ006.why: Every row is matched with every row of the other table. Two tables of 10,000 rows give 100,000,000 rows.
SQ006.fine: A deliberate product with a small table, such as a date spine or a list of scenarios.
SQ006.principle: Every join says how rows match.
SQ006.impact: Performance and correctness. The row count is the product of both tables.
SQ006.check: The join has an `ON`, and the result's row count is what you expect, not the two tables' counts multiplied.
SQ006.before: SELECT o.order_id, c.name FROM dbo.orders o JOIN dbo.customer c
SQ006.after: SELECT o.order_id, c.name FROM dbo.orders o JOIN dbo.customer c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id

SQ007.why: A loop handles one row or batch at a time. A distributed engine is fastest when one statement works on the whole set.
SQ007.fine: Loops over a handful of items, like the tables to load.
SQ007.principle: Work on the whole set in one statement.
SQ007.impact: Performance. Rows are handled one at a time or one batch at a time.
SQ007.check: On a copy of the table, run the loop and the single statement, then check they changed the same rows. Compare the measured times of the two runs.
SQ007.before: -- a cursor that updates each order's status

SQ008.why: A view's `ORDER BY` doesn't order the rows its callers get, and `TOP 10` without `ORDER BY` returns any ten rows, which can change from one run to the next.
SQ008.principle: Order rows where they are returned, and say which rows you want.
SQ008.impact: Reliability. The rows, or their order, can change from one run to the next.
SQ008.check: Running it twice returns the same rows in the same order.
SQ008.before: SELECT TOP 10 customer_id, amount FROM dbo.sales;
SQ008.after: SELECT TOP 10 customer_id, amount FROM dbo.sales ORDER BY amount DESC;

SQ009.why: `GROUP BY` already returns one row per group, so `DISTINCT` only adds a step.
SQ009.principle: Ask for one row per group once.
SQ009.check: Without `DISTINCT`, the query returns the same rows.

SQ010.why: Columns are matched by position. Adding a column to either table, or changing their order, puts values in the wrong columns without an error when the types happen to fit.
SQ010.principle: Match columns by name, never by position.
SQ010.impact: Data quality. Values land in the wrong columns without an error.
SQ010.check: The `INSERT` names its columns, and a few rows of the target table have each value in the right column.
SQ010.before: INSERT INTO dbo.sales_archive SELECT * FROM dbo.sales;
SQ010.after:
INSERT INTO dbo.sales_archive (order_id, order_date, amount)
SELECT order_id, order_date, amount FROM dbo.sales;
